# Housing gap {#sec-gaps} This section quantifies the region's housing shortfall three ways: rental units affordable and available by income band, renters positioned to become owners, and the income required to buy at today's prices. ## Affordable-and-available rental gap by income ::: {.callout-note title="To be added"} An NLIHC-style bar chart of the surplus or deficit of rental units that are both affordable to and available to each AMI band (30/50/80/100/120% AMI), for the region's core three localities (Chesterfield, Henrico, Richmond city). Built from detailed Census microdata, with AMI bands assigned from HUD's FY2026 Income Limits by household size. ::: ## Competition for limited supply of affordable rentals ::: {.callout-note title="To be added"} A table of renter households versus affordable units versus affordable-and-available units by AMI band, showing how higher-income occupancy of low-cost units compounds the shortage at the bottom. Source: detailed Census microdata with HUD's FY2026 Income Limits. ::: ## Starter homes out of reach for most renters ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Most renter households fall short of the income a starter home now requires](gaps_files/figure-html/fig-starter-gap-1.png){#fig-starter-gap fig-align='left' fig-alt='Column chart of renter households in the four primary localities by HUD AMI band, from HUD CHAS 2018-2022 data. Households in the 0-30, 30-50, and 50-80 percent AMI bands are shaded red, marking incomes below what buying the region\'s entry-level home requires. The 80-100 percent AMI band is shaded orange, since the entry-level threshold falls inside that band. The 100 percent and above band is shaded green. Band sizes are roughly 30,500, 24,300, 33,200, 16,700, and 35,000 households.' width=100%} ::: ::: *Below the entry-level threshold: household income under 80 percent of the region's AMI (the 0-30, 30-50, and 50-80 percent bands) — too low to reach the price a starter home requires. Straddles the threshold: the 80-100 percent AMI band, which contains the actual entry-level income threshold (about 88 percent of AMI) — some households in this band clear it, others don't. At or above the threshold: the 100 percent and higher AMI band, which fully clears it.* - **Only about 33% of the region's 139,683 renter households — roughly 45,408 — had income at or above the $99,400 needed to buy the region's entry-level home over the past 12 months.** - That leaves roughly 94,275 renter households priced out of even the least expensive quarter of homes sold regionally, concentrated in the 30,494 households below 30 percent AMI and 24,319 more in the 30-50 percent band. - The entry-level threshold (88 percent of the region's 4-person area median income) falls inside the 80-100 percent AMI band, so even moderate-income renter households only partially clear it. ## What renters need to buy their first home ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Even entry-level homes now require six-figure household income across the board](gaps_files/figure-html/fig-min-income-1.png){#fig-min-income fig-align='left' fig-alt='Column chart showing the share of four-primary-locality households with income at or above what\'s needed to buy the region\'s entry-level, typical, and upper-quartile home, using trailing-12-month MLS sale prices and the current 30-year mortgage rate. Entry-level (25th percentile, $335,000) requires about $99,000 and 45 percent of households qualify. Typical (median, $420,000) requires about $123,000 and 35 percent qualify. Upper quartile ($560,000) requires about $162,000 and 23 percent qualify.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-min-income .cell layout-align="left" tbl-cap='Minimum income needed to buy, by structure type and price point'} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Structure type Price point Sale price Income needed Share of households qualifying
All types Entry-level (25th pct.) $335,000 $99,400 45%
All types Typical (median) $420,000 $123,200 35%
All types Upper (75th pct.) $560,000 $162,500 23%
Single Family Entry-level (25th pct.) $345,000 $102,100 44%
Single Family Typical (median) $439,000 $128,500 33%
Single Family Upper (75th pct.) $599,000 $173,400 21%
Townhouse Entry-level (25th pct.) $325,000 $96,500 46%
Townhouse Typical (median) $385,000 $113,400 39%
Townhouse Upper (75th pct.) $457,600 $133,700 32%
Condominium Entry-level (25th pct.) $280,000 $83,900 53%
Condominium Typical (median) $350,000 $103,600 43%
Condominium Upper (75th pct.) $430,000 $126,000 34%
````` ::: ::: - **Buying the region's median-priced home ($420,000) now takes about $123,200 in household income — only 35% of area households clear that bar.** - Even the entry-level quartile ($335,000) needs about $99,400, out of reach for more than half of the region's households. - Condominiums are the most attainable entry point by structure type; single-family entry-level homes need the most income among the three types at this price tier. - **Assumptions (preliminary):** 10 percent down payment, 30-year fixed term at the current PMMS rate, 1.0 percent of value in annual property tax, and $1,500/year insurance. Not locality-specific. Actual qualifying income will vary with real per-locality tax rates, buyer down payments, and loan products.
